opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in layers. The first layer is the foundation model, which is pretraining at scale. That gave us a huge amount of knowledge and language ability, but for a long time it wasn't clear how to turn it into something that acts in the world. You could chat with it, but chatting is a pretty narrow interface.

The second layer is reasoning. When I was working on things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts, the intuition was simple: if a model can think before it acts, interleave thinking with actions, look at feedback from the environment, and then think again, it starts to generalize much better. Reasoning is what lets the prior knowledge from pretraining actually be used in new situations. Over the past year or two, with reinforcement learning on reasoning, it has finally started working at scale. That's the big shift.

Once you have both a strong prior and reasoning, the question changes. For a long time the field was in what I'd call the "first half." We focused on new methods and models, and we evaluated them on benchmarks. Now the recipe more or less works, so the bottleneck has moved. The important questions are: what tasks should agents actually do, how do we evaluate whether they're useful, and what environments do they live in? I think we're entering the "second half," where defining the problem matters more than the method.

So for the ecosystem, I see a few things happening.

**Environments and interfaces become central.** An agent is only as good as what it can touch: code, browsers, computers, tools, other people. Coding took off first because the environment is clean. You can execute, test, and get feedback. More messy, real-world domains will follow as people build the right interfaces and feedback signals.

**Evaluation has to change.** Many benchmarks assume tasks are independent and fully automatic. Real work is long-horizon and involves humans in the loop. It also has memory and context accumulating over time. If we don't measure that, we'll keep optimizing for the wrong thing.

**Memory and long-term context.** Today most agents are kind of stateless. Each task starts from zero. Humans get better at a job because they accumulate experience. I think some form of lifelong learning or memory is one of the next big unlocks.

**Products and business models.** There's a question of whether agents just become features of existing products, or whether they create new kinds of products and new ways of interacting. My guess is both, but the most interesting value will come from things that weren't possible before, not just making the old workflows a bit faster.

So in short: the foundation model gave us the prior, reasoning made it general, and now the interesting work is about utility. That means figuring out what agents should do in the real world and how we know they're doing it well.

r001.rationale: It separates the earlier focus on new methods and models from later questions about agent interfaces, products, and new ways of interacting.

r002.rationale: It calls memory and lifelong learning a potential unlock, but does not say they are necessary for sustained innovative work over extended periods.

r003.rationale: It discusses reasoning and environmental feedback, but not intrinsic reward sustaining work before external feedback is available.

r004.rationale: It does not describe scalable agent collaboration or agents functioning as an organization.

r005.rationale: It mentions creating new products and interactions, but does not distinguish that from ordinary student-level computer competence in a digital intern.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is that agents are not a separate thing from foundation models and reasoning. They're what you get when those two things are pointed at an environment instead of at a benchmark.

If you look back, the first wave of what people called agents was really prompting. You had a language model, and you wrote some scaffold around it, ReAct-style, think then act then observe, and it looked like an agent. But the model itself hadn't been trained to do any of that. All the intelligence was in the pretrained prior, and all the agent-ness was in the scaffolding. That was fine for demos, but it was fragile, because the model had never actually been optimized on the task of acting in the world.

The second wave, which is roughly where we are now, is that reasoning got pulled into training. Once you can do reinforcement learning on long chains of thought, you can reward a model for actually solving a problem rather than for looking like it solves a problem. And the moment you have that, the distinction between "reasoning" and "acting" starts to dissolve. A tool call is just a thought that has a side effect. A long reasoning trace is just an agent trajectory where all the actions happen to be internal. So I think reasoning models are agents, structurally, and the ecosystem is going to keep converging in that direction.

What that implies for the ecosystem is a shift in where the hard work is. In the prompting era the hard work was in the scaffold. Now I think the hard work is in environments and in evaluation. The models are generic. What's scarce is realistic, verifiable tasks: things with a real reward signal, where you can tell whether the agent succeeded, and where the task actually resembles what people want done. Coding happened to be the first domain where this was true. You have a compiler, you have tests, you have a tight feedback loop, so coding agents got good fast. But that was a property of the environment, not a property of code being special.

So if you ask me what evolving looks like, I'd say: the frontier stops being "can the model reason" and becomes "what can we build a good environment for." Browsing, operating a computer, doing research over days, running experiments. Every domain where someone figures out how to define the task and measure success becomes a domain where agents get strong quite quickly, because the underlying capability is already there and just needs to be shaped.

The other thing I'd say is that the unit of progress changes. For a long time the unit was the model release. I think increasingly it's going to be the task. Someone defines a task well, builds the environment, and then the models fill in. And that's actually good news for people outside the big labs, because defining tasks and building environments is something a lot of people can contribute to, whereas pretraining a frontier model is something very few can.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prompting scaffolds with trained reasoning and discusses user-relevant tasks, but does not distinguish advances in agent methods from advances in how users interact with agent applications.

r002.rationale: It mentions research over days as a possible task, but does not identify long-term memory as necessary for sustained innovative work.

r003.rationale: It discusses reward signals for verifiable tasks, but does not explain that intrinsic reward is needed to sustain work before external feedback is available.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss collaboration among agents or frame scalable collaboration as necessary for organizational function.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish creating new things from ordinary university-student-level computer competence or discuss a digital intern.

astra-6.text:
I think the key shift is from models that answer questions to systems that can actually complete tasks. Foundation models provide the underlying capabilities, and reasoning helps them work through harder problems. But an agent also needs to interact with an environment, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. That feedback loop is essential, because you can’t solve everything by thinking longer before taking an action.

So I would look at the ecosystem in terms of models, environments, and applications. Better models make more tasks possible. Better tools and environments make those capabilities usable. And applications define what success actually means. For an assistant answering a question, success might be a useful response. For an agent, it might be whether the code works or whether a workflow was completed correctly.

One interesting tension is that stronger models may absorb some of the orchestration we build around them today. But that doesn’t mean the application layer disappears. Understanding the user’s task, providing the right context, and making results verifiable still matter. I expect the boundaries to keep moving, with the most useful systems improving through a combination of better reasoning and better interaction with the world.

r001.rationale: It separates model and reasoning improvements from the application layer, including understanding user tasks, supplying context, and verifying results.

r002.rationale: It does not mention long-term memory or sustaining innovative work over extended periods.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss intrinsic reward or sustaining work before external feedback arrives.

r004.rationale: It does not describe collaboration among agents or agents functioning as an organization.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish creating new things from ordinary computer competence expected of a digital intern.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is from models that answer questions to systems that can pursue goals. A foundation model provides a lot of the underlying capability, and reasoning helps it decide what to do. But an agent also needs to act, observe what happened, and adjust. That interaction with the environment is what closes the loop.

So I see model development and agent development reinforcing each other. Better models make more reliable agents possible. At the same time, building agents exposes limitations that are harder to see in a question-answer setting: Can the model recognize a mistake? Can it recover? Can it keep working toward the right objective over many steps?

There’s also a lot of room for work around the model—tools, memory, interfaces, and evaluation. As models improve, some things we currently build into those systems may become model capabilities. But new applications will introduce new requirements. I’d expect the boundary to keep moving.

Ultimately, the important measure is whether an agent can reliably complete useful work. Reasoning is a means toward that, and the ecosystem will develop around turning that capability into dependable outcomes.
